title: BTI: a background reference
summary: A short reference on branch landing pads and the relationship between BTI, PAC, and MTE.
pages:
BTI (T7)




  Deliverable — BTI note (T7, reference only)
  Marius flagged BTI as background, not a workstream, so this is deliberately short.

  Branch Target Identification (BTI) is ARM's coarse control-flow-integrity feature,
  introduced in Armv8.5-A (same architecture version as MTE). It's ARM's analogue to Intel
  CET's indirect-branch tracking (IBT).

           What it does: indirect branches (calls/jumps through a register) may only land on a
           special BTI landing-pad instruction. Jump anywhere else and the CPU faults. This
           stops redirecting an indirect branch into the middle of a function or a ROP/JOP gadget
           that doesn't start with a landing pad.
           How it relates to the rest: BTI is forward-edge CFI (where indirect calls/jumps go).
           PAC's return-address signing is backward-edge CFI (where returns go).
           Complementary, intended to be used together. Neither touches data; both sit at the
           "Hijack" stage, not the "Corrupt" stage where MTE lives.
           Coarse, not fine: BTI only checks the target is a valid landing pad, not the right one. It
           narrows the gadget space rather than eliminating it (much like PAC's default C-
           function-pointer schema allows substitution). A large binary has many landing pads.
           Why it's only reference for us: our targets are heap-memory-safety bugs under MTE
           and Scudo. BTI matters only if an exploit reaches control-flow hijack. For an OOB-read
           disclosure bug like the dav1d candidate, BTI is irrelevant. It becomes relevant only if a
           later target involves a write primitive aiming at a function pointer. Keep it in the back
           pocket.

  To verify when it matters: whether Android ships user-space binaries built with BTI by
  default, and on which devices. Not confirmed — a build-flag question like the PAC-
  coverage one.

title: The research plan
summary: A staged path from a validated harness and baselines to agent evaluation and real targets.
pages:
Plan




  The Refined Plan
  The one question we're answering: how good is an LLM agent at finding and exploiting
  memory-safety bugs — and does a hardened allocator (Scudo + MTE) actually stop it?

  The whole philosophy in one line: start on tiny things we fully control, prove our
  measuring tools work there, then point the agent at real software. Every phase produces
  one checkable thing (an "artifact"), and we don't move on until it holds up. This is what
  keeps us from ever claiming "the agent beat MTE" when the truth was a bug in our own
  setup.


  Word bank (terms used in this plan)

       Term                       Plain meaning

       Agent                      The LLM hooked up to tools (run code, read files,
                                  read crash logs) so it can actually try things, not
                                  just chat.

       Harness                    The scaffolding we build around the agent: runs the
                                  target, feeds it inputs, logs everything.

       Oracle / success-checker   An independent piece of code that decides "did
                                  the attack actually work?" — so the agent can't
                                  grade its own homework.

       Baseline                   A dumb comparison method (random guessing, a
                                  normal fuzzer). The agent has to beat these to be
                                  interesting.

       Fuzzer                     A tool that throws tons of random/mutated inputs
                                  at a program to find crashes. The standard
                                  automated bug-finder.

       Threat model               The written rules of the game: what the attacker
                                  starts with, what counts as winning.

       SYNC / ASYNC               MTE's two modes. SYNC crashes instantly on a bad
                                  access (what we want); ASYNC crashes a moment
                                  later (leaves a gap).




                                                                                        Page 1 of 4

Plan




       Term                       Plain meaning

       Seed                       The random starting value. "Fresh seed" = re-roll
                                  the randomness, to check a win wasn't a fluke.




  The guiding principle
  We are not trying to break MTE. We're measuring whether an LLM agent changes the
  cost, reliability, or range of exploiting a precisely-defined defense. Every phase is built so
  a result can be stated honestly: what the agent was given, what it achieved, and which
  assumption it leaned on.


  Phase 0 — Prove the ruler works (the first thing we build)
  A one-page rules sheet, plus a few tiny buggy programs that let us confirm MTE behaves as
  advertised before any agent is involved.

        Write the threat model: what the attacker starts with, what counts as success, exact
        setup (device/emulator, Android build, Scudo version + commit, tag policy, SYNC vs
        ASYNC).
        Write 3–5 tiny C programs with deliberate bugs — one linear overflow, one use-after-
        free, one tiny intra-granule overflow, one write to an untagged global — each with a
        known expected outcome (which ones MTE should catch, which slip through).
        Build the success-checker and logging before the agent exists.

  Artifact: the rules sheet, the buggy programs, and a passing test showing valid runs work
  and the bugs fault exactly as expected.


  Phase 1 — Measure the dumb baselines
  Get numbers for non-agent methods, so the agent has something to beat.

        Run a random-guess baseline and a normal fuzzer against those same tiny programs.
        Record three rates: did it reach the bug, did it get past MTE, did it achieve a real effect
        — with totals and costs.
        This runs fine on a laptop + emulator; mark anything needing real phone hardware as a
        later confirmation.

  Artifact: a baseline table with error bars (so a lucky run isn't mistaken for a reliable one).


                                                                                               Page 2 of 4

Plan




  Phase 2 — Bring in the agent (still on the tiny programs)
       Give the agent the same programs under the same rules; vary what it starts with
       (source code, just the binary, crash logs) to see what help matters.
       The independent success-checker decides wins. Replay every claimed win from a
       clean start with a fresh seed.
       When it wins, label why: lucky collision, leaked the tag, swapped a pointer, found an
       allocator gap, hit untagged memory, or beat the async window.

  Artifact: the first real comparison — agent vs baselines, broken down by how much help it
  got.


  Phase 3 — Can it redo a known attack?
       Pick one published attack (an easy tag-collision first; a TikTag-style side channel is
       harder and needs real hardware).
       Measure whether the agent can reproduce it within a budget.
       Keep this separate from brand-new tasks, because published attacks may be sitting in
       the model's training data (so reproducing one proves less than discovering one).

  Artifact: a short report stating plainly — did it re-run a known trick, or find something
  new?


  Phase 4 — The real targets (a read, then a write)
  We use two real targets, in order (see the Target tab for full detail):

   1. dav1d / CVE-2025-48592 — the READ target first. Easiest to build, so it de-risks the
      harness. Reason first about whether the bug even survives MTE (likely it becomes a
      crash — a fine result), then run the agent.
   2. Skia / CVE-2025-32318 — the WRITE target second, once the machinery is proven. A
      write gives a clearer "took control" success, exercising the path MTE is really built to
      stop.

  For each: reason about how the bug interacts with MTE, then run the agent under the full
  rules and report all three rates with costs and error bars. Admit each target's drawback
  (dav1d's win is weak; Skia is hard to build and nearer MTE's soft end) — that honesty is
  part of the result.

  Artifact: the end-to-end case studies.

title: Project Zero: MTE as implemented
summary: Notes on known-tag and unknown-tag categories, execution context, and remaining reading.
pages:
Project Zero (T3)




  Deliverable — Project Zero's "MTE As
  Implemented" (T3)
  Mark Brand's three-part Project Zero series (August 2023) treats MTE as a security
  mitigation, not a debugging tool, and lays out a clean taxonomy of how it gets bypassed. I
  read Parts 2 and 3 in full. Part 1 (hardware limits) remains.


  In plain English first
  Google's own elite bug-hunting team (Project Zero) wrote up how well MTE actually holds
  up in the real world. Their verdict: MTE is not an unbreakable wall — it's a speed bump,
  and how tall the bump is depends on where you hit it. It's tallest against a remote attacker
  sending you a malicious file (like our dav1d/Skia targets), and shortest against an attacker
  who can already run code on your phone. This tab is the single best justification for
  picking a remote file-parser as our target.


  Word bank (terms in this tab)

     Term                    Plain meaning

     Mitigation              A defense that makes a bug harder to exploit
                             without fixing the bug itself. MTE is one.

     Known-tag bypass        Attacker learns the color first (usually via a timing
                             trick), then their bad access matches and never
                             crashes.

     Unknown-tag bypass      Attacker wins even with the wrong color, by
                             exploiting a gap (e.g. the async delay).

     Side channel            Learning a secret indirectly — e.g. from how long
                             something takes — instead of reading it directly.

     Speculative execution   The CPU guessing ahead and running code before
                             it's sure it's needed. Attackers abuse the leftovers
                             to leak secrets.

     SYNC / ASYNC            MTE crashing instantly on a bad access vs. a
                             moment later. The delay in ASYNC is a usable gap.




                                                                                          Page 1 of 4

Project Zero (T3)




     Term                     Plain meaning

     Parser                   Code that reads a complex input format (video,
                              image, message). The classic remote attack
                              surface.

     Zygote                   The Android process all apps are forked from. They
                              share a memory layout, which creates a weakness.




  The two bypass classes (adopt this vocabulary)
        Known-tag-bypass. The attacker learns the tag, so their invalid access carries the
        correct tag and never faults. Tag confidentiality is the whole game; a speculative side
        channel breaks it. TikTag and PACMAN are instances.
        Unknown-tag-bypass. The attacker succeeds despite a wrong tag, by exploiting an
        implementation limit (e.g. completing the exploit during the async window before the
        fault is delivered).

  Headline conclusion (paraphrased): using standard memory tagging as a "hard
  probabilistic mitigation" is not generally possible, because wherever an attacker can build
  a speculative side channel, known-tag-bypasses are a fundamental weakness. A citable
  statement of the project's core premise, from Google's own red team.


  SYNC vs ASYNC, sharpened
        ASYNC: results of invalid reads and effects of invalid writes are architecturally
        observable before the fault arrives — what makes unknown-tag-bypasses practical.
        Demonstrated against async-MTE.
        SYNC: invalid reads/writes should not be observable, so unknown-tag-bypasses
        should be rare. SYNC is necessary for any "hard" mitigation.
        Even a "soft" (async) mitigation still inconveniences attackers and raises detection
        risk. "Bypassable" is not "worthless."




                                                                                               Page 2 of 4

Project Zero (T3)

     Context                 Known-tag           Unknown-tag      Takeaway

     renderer)

     escape                  possible                             without syscalls.

                                                                  finish inside one.

     app (remote one-        impossible          bugs very rare   attacker can't easily build a side
     shot)                                                        channel; needs a very good one-

  MTE is strongest against a remote attacker hitting a parser, weakest against a local
  attacker who can run code and build side channels. So a remote-reachable file-format
  parser is the most interesting place to test an agent — and the classic zero-click surface.


  Two concrete Android weaknesses Brand names
    1. .data section pointers are not tagged. With Android's zygote architecture (all apps
        fork from one process, shared layout), pointer-forging between some contexts is easy
        — useful for second-order corruption like type confusion. A coverage gap that needs
        no leak.
    2. Repeated-attempt channels. For a messaging app, known-tag-bypasses are unlikely
       unless the app allows repeated attempts until the tag is correct. The restart question,
        as a concrete app property to check on any target.




                                                                                                  Page 3 of 4

Project Zero (T3)




  Kernel-specific problems (Part 3)
        Tag 0b1111 bypasses checks. The kernel needs TCR_ELx.TCMA1 set, so any pointer
        tagged 0b1111 is dereferenced with no tag check. Forge a tag-15 pointer and you
        sidestep MTE. (In userspace Scudo it's tag 0 that's special; in the kernel it's tag 15.)
        Speculative side channels break kernel tag confidentiality too, plus kernel pointer-
        equality leaks ( kcmp , epoll) and TYPESAFE_BY_RCU regions that require UAF by design
        and can't be tagged.


  What this changes
        Adopt the known-tag / unknown-tag vocabulary in the writeup.
        Target selection should lean toward a remote-reachable parser — where MTE is a real
        obstacle and an agent's bypass is a meaningful result.
        SYNC mode is non-negotiable for the "does MTE stop this" question.
        The .data /zygote pointer-forging gap and the "repeated attempts" property are
        concrete things to check on any candidate.

title: How Scudo uses MTE
summary: Source-reading notes on memtag.h, tagging instructions, exclusions, check suppression, and the separate PA question.
pages:
Scudo + MTE (T4)




  Deliverable — Reading Scudo's memtag.h
  (T4)
  I read the actual Scudo memtag.h source (the LLVM copy Android builds from). This
  confirms several things the guide marked unverified, and answers "how does Scudo use
  MTE" at the instruction level. Caveat: this is main , not a pinned Android release — for the
  real audit (Phase 0) pin the exact commit for your target build. Mechanisms are stable;
  constants can move.


  In plain English first
  Scudo is Android's malloc — the code that hands out memory. MTE is a hardware feature
  that stamps a tiny color on each piece of memory and crashes the program if a pointer's
  color doesn't match. The point of this tab: MTE is just the hardware check; Scudo is the
  code that actually chooses the colors and stamps them. I read Scudo's real source to
  confirm exactly how it does that — and to settle whether it also uses PA (it doesn't). The
  three things that matter: tag 0 is always skipped (so odds are 1-in-15, not 1-in-16), there's a
  switch that turns checks off for speed (an audit target), and there is zero Pointer
  Authentication in the allocator.


  Word bank (terms in this tab)

     Term               Plain meaning

     Allocator          The library behind malloc / free that hands out
                        and reclaims memory. Scudo is Android's.

     Tag / color        The 4-bit value MTE stamps on memory and
                        pointers. "Color" is just my nickname for it.

     Granule            The 16-byte unit of memory that gets one tag.

     IRG / STG / STZG   ARM instructions: pick a random tag / stamp a tag /
                        stamp-and-zero. Scudo calls these.

     PSTATE.TCO         A CPU switch that temporarily turns tag-checking
                        off. Scudo flips it in a few spots for speed.




                                                                                            Page 1 of 4

Scudo + MTE (T4)




     Term                 Plain meaning

     PA / PAC             Pointer Authentication — a separate feature that
                          signs pointers. Confirmed: not used by Scudo.

     Pinned commit        A specific frozen version of the source. We must
                          pin one for the real audit, since code changes over
                          time.

     prctl / HWCAP2       Linux calls that check "does this CPU support
                          MTE?" and "turn MTE on for this process."




  Confirmed: tag 0 is always excluded
  In selectRandomTag , the first line is literally ExcludeMask |= 1 , with the comment
  "Always exclude Tag 0." So the random tag is drawn from 15 values, not 16.

  This is why Project Zero and the AOSP docs say 1/15, not 1/16. Use 1/15 (≈6.7%) as the per-
  attempt collision chance against a random tag.


  Confirmed: check suppression via PSTATE.TCO
   ScopedDisableMemoryTagChecks is a C++ scope guard: on construction it reads the
  current TCO bit and sets msr tco, #1 (tag-check-override on); on destruction it
  restores. While alive, tag checks are off for that thread.

  The concrete audit target: any path that runs inside one of these scopes performs
  memory accesses with no tag checking. The question for an attacker/agent: can attacker-
  influenced data be processed inside such a scope? Greppable: every construction of
   ScopedDisableMemoryTagChecks , and what runs in its lifetime.



  How the tagging actually works
  The core is setRandomTag(Ptr, Size, ExcludeMask, ...) :

   1. Pick the tag: selectRandomTag runs IRG , inserting a hardware-chosen random tag
      into the pointer's top byte, honoring the exclude mask (always includes tag 0).
   2. Paint the memory: storeTags(Begin, End) writes that tag across the allocation. Fast
       path: STZG (store-tag-and-zero, one granule) to a cache-line boundary, then DC GZVA
       (tag-and-zero a whole cache line) for the bulk, then STZG for the tail. So allocation


                                                                                               Page 2 of 4

Scudo + MTE (T4)




       memory is tagged and zeroed together. Slow path (plain STZG loop) when the region is
       small or DC is unavailable.

  Other primitives:

        extractTag(Ptr) = (Ptr >> 56) & 0xf — pull the 4-bit tag from bits 56–59.

        untagPointer(Ptr) = Ptr & ((1<<56)-1) — strip the tag.
        addFixedTag(Ptr, Tag) — set a specific tag (deterministic, not random).

        storeTag (single STG ), loadTag ( LDG ).
       Granule size hard-coded to 16 bytes; minimum alignment ≥ one granule.

  Mental model confirmed: Scudo picks a random non-zero tag with IRG , paints it over the
  allocation (zeroing as it goes) with STZG / DC GZVA , returns the tagged pointer, retags on
  free. Hardware checks; Scudo does all policy.


  Confirmed: no Pointer Authentication in this file
  There is no PA, no PAC, no PAC / AUT instruction anywhere in memtag.h . Tagging only.
  This settles the open question: Scudo's MTE path does not itself use PA. So when Marius
  says "how Scudo integrates MTE and PA," the PA part is almost certainly not inside the
  allocator's tagging code. It's most likely:

       compiler-generated return-address signing (RET PAC) in the binaries that call Scudo —
       and Project Zero's Pixel 10 post confirmed Pixel 10 uses RET PAC in place of the stack
       protector; or
       a separate platform layer; or
       something Marius wants to add or evaluate.

  The sharp question for Marius: "I read Scudo's memtag.h; it's MTE-only, no PAC. So when

summary: The foundational guide: vocabulary, mitigation mechanics, literature, research design, and a glossary.

Study Guide




  Memory Hardening & LLMs: A Newcomer's
  Study Guide
    Oct 6, 2026   · ​@Shaurya


  0. How to use this guide
  The project asks one question: hardware defenses like MTE and PAC make exploitation
  "probabilistically hard" for humans, but does that still hold when an LLM agent is the
  attacker? Everything below builds the vocabulary and the mental models you need to
  discuss that question with Marius on Wednesday.

  The one-paragraph version. C and C++ programs have memory bugs. Attackers turn
  those bugs into control over a device. Over decades, defenders added software and
  hardware barriers. The newest barriers (Arm's Memory Tagging Extension and Pointer
  Authentication) work by attaching small secret values to memory and pointers, so a
  wrong guess crashes the program. Because the secrets are small (4 bits for MTE, roughly
  7 to 16 bits for PAC), a lucky guess is possible but unlikely. Marius wants to know whether
  an LLM changes that math in practice, by lowering the cost of attempts, spotting leaks, or
  finding places where the defense is not actually applied.

  How I labeled things. I read both of Marius's articles in full today (October 6, 2026).
  Claims taken from them are marked Apple says or Android says. Claims from my own
  background knowledge are marked Background. My own reasoning is marked Inference.
  Things to ask Marius are marked Ask.

  What I did not independently verify. The Codex brief you pasted cites several other
  sources (Marius's website, his papers, Linux and Clang documentation, the PACMAN,
  TikTag and StickyTags papers). I use its claims where noted, but treat paper details as "to
  confirm when you read them."


  Reading paths by time available

     Time you have     Read these sections         Skip for now

     30 minutes        0, 2, 6, 10, 12             Everything else

     2 hours           0 through 4, 6, 7, 10, 12   5, 9, 11 (skim)




                                                                                         Page 1 of 48

Study Guide




     Time you have   Read these sections      Skip for now

     Full evening    All, in order            Nothing



  How the sections connect
  Sections 1 to 4 are the foundation: security vocabulary, memory bugs, how bugs become
  exploits, and the defenses that came before. Sections 5 to 8 are the technology Marius
  named: allocators and Scudo, MTE, PA, and Apple's combined system. Section 9 covers
  known attacks on those defenses. Section 10 is the research question itself. Section 11 is
  about Marius and his papers, and section 12 is meeting prep. Section 13 is a glossary you
  can search any time a word trips you up, and section 14 holds the reading order and
  sources.


  1. Security vocabulary for a newcomer
  Security papers are mostly careful statements of who can do what to whom. If you master
  six words (asset, attacker, vulnerability, exploit, mitigation, threat model) you can read
  most of the abstracts you will meet.


  The core words

     Term              Plain meaning                         Example in this project

     Asset             What the defender wants to            A phone user's messages and
                       protect                               photos

     Attacker          Whoever is trying to break in, plus   An app the user installed, or a
                       what they can already do              malicious web page

     Vulnerability     A mistake in the program that         Writing 17 bytes into a 16-byte
     (bug)             could be abused                       buffer

     Exploit           Code or input that turns a            A crafted image file that makes
                       vulnerability into attacker benefit   the phone run attacker code

     Mitigation        A defense that makes exploiting a     MTE, PAC, ASLR
                       bug harder without removing the
                       bug




                                                                                               Page 2 of 48

Study Guide




     Term             Plain meaning                          Example in this project

     Threat model     The written assumptions about          "Attacker has a memory-write bug
                      attacker abilities, goals and limits   and can retry freely, but cannot
                                                             read tags"

     Attack surface   Every place attacker-controlled        Web content, messages, file
                      input enters                           parsers, system calls

     Privilege        A line the attacker wants to cross     App to kernel, browser tab to the
     boundary                                                rest of the OS



  Ideas that matter more than the definitions
  A mitigation is not a fix. The bug is still in the code. The mitigation changes what the bug
  lets an attacker do. This is why Apple's article keeps talking about making chains "more
  expensive and difficult to develop and maintain" rather than impossible. Apple says its
  goal is to disrupt mercenary spyware, which chains several bugs together at a cost of
  millions of dollars.

  An exploit chain is a sequence of steps. A realistic attack might start with a bug in a web
  page renderer, escape the renderer's sandbox, then attack the kernel. Each step needs its
  own bug and its own technique. Apple says a defense that breaks one early step can
  invalidate the whole chain, and the attacker must start over with new bugs.

  Deterministic versus probabilistic defenses. A deterministic defense blocks an attack
  outright, for example a guard page that always faults. A probabilistic defense blocks it
  most of the time, and the attacker wins only by luck. MTE with 4-bit tags and PAC with
  short signatures are probabilistic. That is exactly why Marius's question is interesting.

  A crash is information. When a wrong guess crashes the program, the attacker learns
  something (the guess was wrong) and the defender also learns something (an attack
  happened, logs are written). Whether the attacker can try again depends on whether the
  target restarts, and whether the secret changes after a restart. Much of the research
  literature is really about this one question: does a failed attempt cost the attacker
  anything?

  An oracle is anything that answers a question about a secret. If an attacker can ask "is
  this tag correct?" and get an answer without crashing, that is an oracle, and it turns a 1-in-
  16 gamble into a cheap search. Speculative execution attacks (section 9) are oracles that
  do not crash the process.




                                                                                           Page 3 of 48

Study Guide




  Reliability matters as much as possibility. An exploit that works 1 time in 16 and crashes
  the other 15 is very different from one that works every time. Papers report success rates
  and time to success, not just "it works."


  Names you will see in papers
       CVE: an identifier for a specific publicly known vulnerability.
       CWE: a catalog of bug types. CWE-787 is out-of-bounds write. CWE-416 is use-after-
       free.
       PoC (proof of concept): minimal code showing a bug or attack works.
       Sandbox: an environment that restricts what code can do, so compromising it does not
       immediately compromise the system.


  2. Memory safety bugs from first principles
  Every memory safety bug is a violation of one of two questions: is this access inside the
  object it was meant for, and is that object still alive? The first is a spatial question and the
  second is a temporal one. MTE exists to catch both.


  Background: what memory looks like to a program
  Memory is a long array of bytes, each with a numeric address. A pointer is a variable that
  holds an address. On a 64-bit phone, a pointer is 64 bits wide.

  Programs get memory in two main places. The stack holds local variables and return
  addresses, and is managed automatically as functions are called and return. The heap
  holds memory a program requests explicitly with malloc (C) or new (C++) and releases
  with free or delete . Heap bugs are the focus of this project, because the heap allocator
  (section 5) is where MTE tagging happens.

  C and C++ do not check that a pointer stays inside its object, and do not track whether
  the object is still alive. That freedom is why they are fast, and why they have these bugs.


  Spatial errors: going out of bounds

     char *buf = malloc(16);        // valid indices: 0..15
     buf[16] = 'A';                 // one byte past the end: out-of-bounds write




                                                                                             Page 4 of 48

Study Guide




  The write lands on whatever sits next to the buffer. That might be another heap object,
  allocator bookkeeping, or unused padding. Writes are usually more dangerous than reads
  because they change program state, though out-of-bounds reads can leak secrets such as
  pointers or keys.

  A common real-world cause is length arithmetic: a program computes a size, the
  computation overflows or is attacker-influenced, and a copy writes too many bytes.


  Temporal errors: use after free

     struct User *u = malloc(sizeof *u);
     free(u);                  // the allocator may now reuse this memory
     struct Msg *m = malloc(sizeof *m); // may land at the same address as u
     u->is_admin = 1;          // stale pointer now writes into m


  The pointer u still holds the old address. The program has a dangling pointer. If the
  allocator gave the same memory to a new object, the stale write corrupts the new object.
  Setting u = NULL only fixes that one pointer. If other pointers (aliases) still refer to the
  same memory, they remain dangling.


  Other bug types you will hear about
       Double free: freeing the same allocation twice, which can corrupt allocator state.
       Type confusion: treating an object as the wrong type, so field offsets mean something
       different.
       Integer overflow: arithmetic that wraps around and leads to a too-small allocation or a
       too-large copy.
       Uninitialized memory: reading bytes that were never set, which can leak old data.
       Intra-object overflow: overflowing from one field into another field inside the same
       allocation. This one matters a lot later, because tag checks cannot see it (section 6).


  Why not just switch languages?
  Memory-safe languages like Rust and Swift check bounds and lifetimes. Apple says it uses
  Swift for new code and targeted rewrites, while also deploying mitigations at scale.
  Billions of lines of existing C and C++ are not going away soon, which is why hardware-
  assisted hardening matters. (Marius's Crustify project, according to the Codex brief, uses
  an LLM harness for Rust migration.)




                                                                                            Page 5 of 48

Study Guide




  The five-stage vocabulary
  The Codex brief proposes a vocabulary I recommend adopting, because it prevents
  sloppy claims:

   1. Bug: the program violates its intended memory rules.
   2. Trigger: an input or sequence that reaches the bug.
   3. Primitive: a useful capability the bug provides, such as "write 8 controlled bytes at an
       adjacent object."
   4. Security effect: the capability crosses a stated security boundary.
   5. Reliable exploit: the effect is reproducible under the declared conditions.

  A crash alone is only stage 1 or 2. A tag-fault means the defense worked. A "successful
  bypass" has to get to stage 4 at least.


  3. From bug to exploit
  An exploit is the engineering work of turning a small mistake (one bad write) into a reliable
  capability (running attacker code or changing a security decision). Defenses like MTE and
  PAC are designed to break specific steps of that process, so you need a rough picture of
  the steps.


  Primitives: what a bug gives the attacker
  Security researchers describe a bug by the capability it hands over, called a primitive:

       Relative write: write attacker-chosen bytes at some offset from a known object (a
       typical overflow).
       Arbitrary read: read any address the attacker names. This defeats secrecy.
       Arbitrary write: write any bytes to any address the attacker names. This is usually
       game over.
       Information leak: learn an address or secret value without any corruption.

  Exploit development is largely about upgrading a weak primitive into a stronger one. A
  one-byte relative write might be used to corrupt a length field, which then allows a bigger
  read, which leaks a pointer, which enables an arbitrary write.




                                                                                          Page 6 of 48

Study Guide




  Heap grooming (heap feng shui)
  Because the heap allocator decides where objects go, attackers manipulate the sequence
  of allocations and frees so the victim lands where they want. A typical use-after-free
  recipe:

   1. Trigger the allocation of a victim object of some size.
   2. Trigger its free while a dangling pointer remains.
   3. Allocate many attacker-controlled objects of the same size, hoping one reclaims that
      slot.
   4. Use the dangling pointer. It now reads or writes the attacker's object, interpreted as
       the victim type.

  Apple says the attacker's goal in both use-after-free and out-of-bounds bugs is to create
  "overlapping interpretations of memory" by controlling where certain allocations land.
  This is precisely what typed allocators and tagging try to prevent.


  Two flavors of end goal
  Control-flow hijack. Overwrite something that decides where the program jumps next: a
  return address, a function pointer, or a C++ virtual table entry. Modern attackers rarely
  inject new code. They reuse existing code fragments in a technique called return-oriented
  programming (ROP). Background: Pointer Authentication was designed to make forged
  return addresses and function pointers fail.

  Data-only attack. Change a variable that the program trusts, such as a permission flag, a
  file path, or an object's length, without redirecting execution at all. This is important for
  the project: a defense that protects code pointers does nothing against a corrupted
   is_admin field unless something else protects that field. The Codex brief calls this a
  "data-only effect."


  The role of information leaks
  Many defenses depend on a secret the attacker does not know: where code lives (ASLR),
  the PAC signature, the MTE tag. Attackers therefore often need a leak first. In MTE
  research, the key question is whether tags can be learned without causing a fault. Apple's
  article spends a full section on this, which it calls Tag Confidentiality Enforcement.




                                                                                            Page 7 of 48

Study Guide




  Where each defense interrupts the pipeline




  attack pipeline and the defenses aimed at each step

  Read left to right: a defense that breaks an early step forces the attacker to restart with a
  different bug. The table below adds what the attacker does at each step.


     Stage      What the attacker does                  Defense aimed at it

     Layout     Groom the heap so objects are           Typed allocators, randomization,
                adjacent or reused                      quarantine

     Corrupt    Perform the out-of-bounds or stale      MTE (tag mismatch faults)
                access

     Leak       Learn addresses and secrets             ASLR, tag confidentiality, side-channel
                                                        mitigations

     Hijack     Redirect execution                      PAC, control-flow integrity

     Effect     Gain code execution or change a         Sandboxing, privilege separation
                security decision



  Why this matters for the LLM question
  Every row above involves reading code, forming a plan, writing helper code, running it, and
  interpreting crashes. These are tasks LLM agents are being applied to. Inference: an agent
  is most plausibly useful at (a) the search-heavy parts like heap layout experimentation,
  (b) understanding unfamiliar allocator code, and (c) iterating on crash feedback. It is least
  obviously useful at guessing a truly random secret, because no amount of reasoning
  improves a blind 1-in-16 guess. Distinguishing these cases is the heart of the project.


                                                                                            Page 8 of 48

Study Guide




  4. Classic mitigations and why they were not enough
  MTE and PAC are the third generation of memory defenses. Knowing the earlier
  generations explains why the industry moved to hardware, and gives you comparison
  points for Wednesday.


  Generation 1: make the easy attacks fail

     Mitigation        What it does                          How attackers got around it

     Stack canary      Places a secret value before the      Leak the canary first, or corrupt
                       return address and checks it          data that does not cross it
                       before returning

     NX / DEP (no-     Memory is writable or executable,     Reuse existing code with ROP
     execute)          never both, so injected code will     instead of injecting new code
                       not run

     ASLR              Randomizes where code and data        Leak one pointer to recompute
                       load, so addresses are unknown        the layout

     Guard pages       Unmapped pages around large           Only helps at page granularity, not
                       allocations fault on overflow         for small objects


  None of these detect the bug itself. They make exploitation harder, and attackers adapted
  by chaining an information leak with ROP.


  Generation 2: control-flow protections
  Control-flow integrity (CFI) restricts where indirect jumps and calls may go. Shadow
  stacks keep a protected copy of return addresses. Pointer Authentication (section 7)
  achieves a similar goal using cryptographic signatures stored in the pointers themselves.
  Apple says it was first to deploy PAC, in the A12 Bionic chip in 2018, and that its success in
  raising exploitation complexity convinced Apple that deep hardware and software
  integration would be key.

  The weakness shared by this generation: they protect where code goes, not what data
  holds. Data-only attacks and many heap corruptions pass straight through.




                                                                                             Page 9 of 48

Study Guide




  Generation 3: detect the memory error itself
  The idea is to catch the out-of-bounds or stale access at the moment it happens. Three
  tools you will see named together on the Android NDK pages:

       AddressSanitizer (ASan): the compiler adds checks around memory accesses, using
       "shadow memory" to track which bytes are valid. It is accurate but slow and memory-
       hungry, so it is a testing tool.
       HWAddress Sanitizer (HWASan): a software implementation of the tagging idea.
       Pointers carry a tag and the compiler inserts tag checks. Lower overhead than ASan
       but still requires recompiling. Android says MTE SYNC mode is a faster alternative that
       does not require recompiling.
       MTE: the same tagging idea implemented in hardware, so every load and store is
       checked by the CPU at low cost.

  Background: GWP-ASan, also listed in the NDK menu, is a sampling tool that protects a
  small random fraction of allocations to find bugs in production. It is cheap because it only
  checks a few allocations.


  The trade-off triangle
  Every memory defense balances three things: coverage (how many bugs it catches), cost
  (CPU, memory, battery), and strength (whether a determined attacker can get around it).
  Tools that are strong and complete (ASan) cost too much to ship. Cheap tools (canaries)
  are weak. MTE's pitch is to move that frontier, giving broad coverage at low cost, with the
  price being that its strength is probabilistic.


  Why attackers kept winning
  Apple says known mercenary spyware chains against iOS, Windows and Android share
  one trait: they exploit memory safety vulnerabilities, which it describes as
  "interchangeable, powerful, and exist throughout the industry." Interchangeable is the key
  word. If a defense only blocks one bug's exploitation, attackers swap in another bug. A
  defense must take away a technique (such as "overlap a freed object with an attacker
  object") to matter. That is the framing for evaluating MTE, PAC and Scudo in this project.




                                                                                         Page 10 of 48

Study Guide




  5. Allocators and Scudo
  The allocator is the library behind malloc and free , and it is where MTE tagging actually
  happens. The hardware only checks tags; the allocator decides what tags to assign. That
  makes allocator policy as important to security as the hardware feature.


  What an allocator does
  A program asks for N bytes. The allocator finds a free region, hands back a pointer, and
  remembers enough to take it back when free is called. Fast allocators keep size classes
  (separate pools for 16-byte, 32-byte, 48-byte objects and so on) and free lists (recently
  freed blocks, ready for reuse). Reuse is the property attackers exploit: a freed slot is likely
  to be the next allocation of the same size.

  Allocators also store metadata (size, state, links between free blocks). If that metadata
  sits right next to user data, an overflow can corrupt it. Much classic heap exploitation
  targets allocator metadata. This is why Marius's ISLAB paper is about protecting memory-
  management metadata.


  Scudo: Android's hardened allocator
  Background and LLVM docs say: Scudo is a user-mode allocator based on LLVM's sanitizer
  allocator, designed to add mitigations against heap vulnerabilities while keeping
  performance reasonable. It is the default on Fuchsia and, per the docs, on Android since
  Android 11. The name is Italian for "shield."

  Its components, as the LLVM docs describe them:


     Component                       Role

     Primary allocator               Fast path for smaller sizes. Carves reserved
                                     regions into identical-size blocks, one region per
                                     size class.

     Secondary allocator             Slower path for large sizes. Uses OS memory
                                     mapping, with guard pages around each allocation.

     Thread-specific data registry   Controls per-thread caches, either exclusive per
                                     thread or a shared fixed pool.




                                                                                           Page 11 of 48

Study Guide




     Component                     Role

     Quarantine                    Delays reuse of freed blocks to blunt use-after-
                                   free. Costly, and disabled by default in the
                                   documented defaults ( quarantine_size_kb is 0).



  The chunk header and its checksum
  Every chunk Scudo hands out is preceded by an 8-byte header. It stores the size class, the
  chunk's state (available, allocated or quarantined), the allocation type ( malloc , new ,
   new[] , memalign ), size information, an offset back to the underlying block, and a 16-bit
  checksum.

  The checksum is a CRC32 computed over a global secret, the chunk's own pointer, and
  the header bytes. The docs say plainly that it is not intended to be cryptographically
  strong, and that corruption is only detected when the header is next accessed. So an
  overflow that damages a header but never touches it again goes unnoticed.

  Do not confuse this checksum with Pointer Authentication. It is a software integrity
  check in the allocator, not an Arm PAC. Section 7 and the meeting questions return to this,
  because the sources I read do not say how (or whether) Scudo uses PA.


  Randomness and other hardening
  Scudo randomizes how blocks are chosen in the Primary allocator, and can randomize how
  caches are assigned to threads. The docs note that it trusts the OS and ASLR for
  unpredictable page placement, and that security "will be greatly reduced" if that
  assumption fails. Optional features include zero-filling or pattern-filling memory on
  allocation, and checks for mismatched allocation and deallocation types (for example
  malloc paired with delete ).

  When Scudo detects trouble it prints an error beginning "Scudo ERROR" and may
  terminate the process. Messages you will see include corrupted chunk header (checksum
  failed), invalid chunk state (typical for a double free), and misaligned pointer (alignment is
  16 bytes on 64-bit).


  How Scudo and MTE connect
  Three facts from the Scudo and Android pages:




                                                                                          Page 12 of 48

Study Guide




        M_MEMTAG_TUNING is a mallopt option that tunes how Scudo picks tags, so that a
       certain class of memory error is more likely to be caught (details in section 6).
       In SYNC mode, Scudo records the stack trace of allocations and deallocations so fault
       reports can explain what happened. The LLVM docs describe an
        allocation_ring_buffer_size option (default 32768) controlling how many past
       allocations are kept for this.
       The sample crash report on the Android NDK page shows frames named like
       scudo::Allocator::deallocate and quarantineOrDeallocateChunk . That function
       name does not mean the quarantine is enabled; the docs say it is off by default.


  What to take away
  Inference: a Scudo assessment has at least three layers worth separating: (1) allocator
  logic and its checks, such as header checksum and state checks, (2) MTE tag assignment
  policy, and (3) the places where tag checking is bypassed or suspended. Marius's plan to
  look at "how Scudo integrates MTE and PA" probably spans all three. Ask: which Scudo
  revision and which Android build.


  6. Memory Tagging Extension (MTE) in depth
  MTE is a lock-and-key system for memory: every chunk of memory gets a small "color"
  (the lock), every pointer to it carries the same color (the key), and the CPU faults when
  they do not match. This is the single most important section for the project, so read it
  twice.


  The mechanism
       Memory is divided into 16-byte granules. Each granule has a hidden 4-bit allocation
       tag (16 possible values), stored by the hardware outside normal addressable memory.
       A pointer carries a 4-bit logical tag in its otherwise unused top bits (bits 59 to 56, per
       the Codex brief and the Linux documentation it cites). The mechanism that lets the
       CPU ignore those top bits for addressing is called Top Byte Ignore.
       On every load and store, the CPU compares the pointer's tag with the granule's tag. A
       match proceeds. A mismatch is a tag check fault, and what happens next depends on
       the mode.




                                                                                             Page 13 of 48

Study Guide




  Android says MTE is a hardware extension that catches use-after-free and buffer-
  overflow bugs. Apple says each allocation "is tagged with a secret" and the hardware
  grants access only when the request carries the right one. Both descriptions match the
  model above.


  How the allocator uses it
  The NDK guide's section for people writing their own allocator shows what the allocator
  must do, and therefore what the hardware gives it:

   1. Map pages with PROT_MTE so the OS enables tagging for them.
   2. Align every tagged allocation to 16 bytes, because tags apply to 16-byte granules.
   3. Pick a random tag with the IRG instruction and place it in the returned pointer.
   4. Write that tag onto the memory with STG (one granule), ST2G (two), or DC GVA (a
       whole cache line). The STZG , STZ2G and DC GZVA variants also zero the memory.
   5. On free , retag the memory so old pointers no longer match.


  A worked example
  Three adjacent 32-byte allocations, A, B and C, are given tags 3, 9 and 5. The pointers pA ,
  pB , pC carry those tags.

        pA[0] reads a granule tagged 3 through a pointer tagged 3. Match. Allowed.

        pA[32] runs off the end of A into B's granule, tagged 9. The pointer says 3, the memory
       says 9. Fault. This is how MTE catches a linear overflow.
       The program frees B. The allocator retags B's memory, say to 12. A stale pB still says 9.
       pB[0] now compares 9 against 12. Fault. This is how MTE catches use-after-free.
       Now suppose the random re-tag happened to pick 9 again. Then pB[0] matches and

  Under an illustrative model (a hidden tag uniform over 16 values, independent fresh

  guess against the same fixed tag is not a fresh independent trial. So the real questions
  are: does the target restart, are tags re-randomized, and can the attacker learn the tag

  7. Pointer Authentication (PA, PAC, PAuth)
  Pointer Authentication puts a short cryptographic signature inside a pointer, so that a
  pointer forged or modified by an attacker fails verification before it is used. Where MTE
  asks "is this memory access allowed?", PA asks "is this pointer the one the program itself
  created for this purpose?" I read the Linux kernel documentation and Clang's Pointer
  Authentication manual for this section.

  Why the discriminator matters
  Without a discriminator, an attacker could copy any validly signed pointer to any other
  place that expects a pointer signed with the same key. Mixing in context prevents that.
  Common choices:

       Storage address (address diversity): a pointer stored at address X only validates
       when read from X, so copying it elsewhere fails.
       A constant tied to purpose or type: for example Clang signs C++ virtual functions
       using a hash of the method's name and signature.
       The stack pointer: Clang says on Apple's arm64e ABI the return address is signed with
       the IB key using the stack pointer at function entry as the discriminator.


  How big is the signature?
  The signature has to fit in the pointer's unused bits, so its width depends on how many
  address bits the system uses. Linux docs say the PAC width is 55 minus the configured
  virtual address size, and that with a 48-bit address space the PAC is 7 bits wide. The IUBIK
  paper reports a concrete case: on a Pixel 8 running a Linux 5.15 kernel, virtual addresses
  use bits 0 to 38, MTE tags use bits 56 to 59, and the PAC gets 16 bits (bits 39 to 54). That is
  a kernel configuration, so userspace may differ. This is where the "7 to 16 bits" range
  comes from; IUBIK also notes that PAC length can range from 3 to 31 bits depending on
  hardware configuration. If the signature were uniformly unpredictable and b bits wide, a
  blind guess succeeds with probability 2 to the power of minus b: 1 in 128 at 7 bits, 1 in
  65,536 at 16 bits.

  Keys
  Linux docs say the extension provides five keys: two for instruction addresses (APIAKey,
  APIBKey), two for data addresses (APDAKey, APDBKey), and one generic key (APGAKey).
  The kernel assigns random keys to each process at exec . The keys are shared across
  threads in the process and preserved across fork() . Userspace can request new keys
  with the PR_PAC_RESET_KEYS option of prctl .

  The fact that child processes keep their parent's keys after fork is a classic reason
  brute-force attacks on forking servers are interesting: each crash and respawn does not
  reset the secret. Compare MTE, where tags are chosen per allocation at runtime.


  What happens on failure
  Baseline Armv8.3 aut instructions do not trap by themselves. They corrupt the pointer
  so that a later use probably faults. With the optional FPAC extension, failure traps
  immediately. Clang says this difference matters for security: if the failure only shows up
  later, and the kernel lets the process recover from the resulting fault, the attacker may be
  able to build an authentication oracle that tells them whether a guess was valid without
  ending the process.

  control of execution. In Clang's design:

  How PACMAN works, step by step
  The PACMAN authors describe a clean recipe that generalizes beyond PAC:

   1. Start with an ordinary memory read/write bug. It lets the attacker supply a guess for
       the PAC on a pointer.
   2. Find a gadget in the victim: code that authenticates a pointer and then uses it, but only
      on a conditional path the attacker can steer.
   3. Run the guess speculatively. The CPU executes the path ahead of time, and if the
       guess was wrong, it throws the work away without raising a visible crash.
   4. Read the result through a side channel. PACMAN watches whether the speculative
       load evicted entries from the TLB (a technique called prime+probe). Eviction suggests
       the PAC was right.
   5. Repeat for every possible PAC value. The PAC space is small, so brute force is feasible.

  Read IUBIK first
  IUBIK is the paper to read before Wednesday, because it is the only one that uses MTE
  and PA together. Here is what it does, in plain language.

  The observation. The authors analyzed kernel exploits from 2020 to 2024 and found most
  share a trick: use a limited memory bug (use-after-free or out-of-bounds) to overlap a
  user-controlled object with a sensitive kernel object. User-controlled objects, which the
  paper calls usercopy primitives, are objects the attacker can fill with chosen bytes
  through calls like copy_from_user . Instead of trying to list every sensitive object to
  protect (which keeps failing), IUBIK isolates the attacker-controlled objects.

  The mechanism.

   1. Two MTE domains. Kernel heap pages are tagged with one of exactly two tags: TagU
       for user-controlled objects, TagK for everything else. Access across the boundary
       faults. The paper uses synchronous mode. Because it needs only two tags, it avoids the
       limitation of having just 16 tags, which it says raised concerns in prior work, including
       StickyTags.

   2. Struct rewriting. Many kernel structs mix attacker-controlled bytes with sensitive
       fields such as function pointers. IUBIK splits such a struct into two objects, putting the
       user bytes in the TagU domain and the sensitive rest in TagK. The paper reports
       rewriting 29 structs in total.
   3. A PAC-protected back-reference. When code needs to go from the extracted part
       back to the original object (the container_of idiom), the paper keeps a backward
       pointer and protects it with PA: signed with PACDA , checked with AUTDA , using the
       pointer's storage address as context to stop replay. This is the "PA" use in this paper.
   4. A profiler. A dynamic tool finds allocation sites where user data lands. It recorded 292
      privileged and 212 non-privileged allocation sites across the workloads they ran.

  The results. On a Pixel 8 with an Android 14 kernel (Linux 5.15), the prototype showed
  worst-case slowdowns of 7% to 8% on two micro-benchmarks and under 3% on macro-
  benchmarks, with 2.17% more memory at boot (about 7 MB). In a survey of 31 public
  exploits from the previous five years, the paper says 28 (90.3%) would be mitigated.
  Three would not, for reasons the authors discuss.

  The scope and the caveats that matter to you. Pay close attention to the threat model
  section.

       The attacker can trigger memory errors as often as they like, but side-channel,
       microarchitectural and fault-injection attacks are out of scope. That is exactly where

       The design requires that MTE and PA cannot be disabled.
       The authors list weaknesses they have not seen in any exploit: attackers might overlap
       pointers between the two domains, corrupt them, or use a write primitive on a
       sensitive object (such as process credentials) obtained without usercopy primitives.
       The conference meta-review noted possible bypasses had not been demonstrated,
       and that profiler accuracy is not guaranteed.
       The authors suggest the idea could port to user space, with the Heartbleed bug (a
       heap over-read in OpenSSL) as an example of what isolating attacker-controlled input
       could prevent.

  Deliverable — The Real-World Target (T1)
  The job: pick a real, recently-broken piece of Android software to point our LLM agent at,
  and reason about whether its bug still works once the hardened allocator (Scudo + MTE)

     Term                   Plain meaning

     OOB read               You read memory you shouldn't → leaks secrets.

Target (T1)




  Target A — dav1d (CVE-2025-48592): the READ target
  What it is: a heap out-of-bounds read in C2SoftDav1dDec.cpp , Android's wrapper around
  dav1d (the AV1 video decoder). A crafted video makes the decoder read past a buffer and
  leak memory. Remote, zero-click, Android 15/16, patched Dec 2025, CVSS 7.5.

  Why it's a good target:

        It's C/C++ on ARM, runs on Scudo — exactly our setup.
        Remote and zero-click: the strongest, most realistic attack surface.
        It's one small, self-contained decoder, so we can build it and reproduce the bug in an
        afternoon — ideal for getting our test harness working.
        There's a patch commit to compare against, so we can see the bug precisely.

  Does the bug survive MTE? (the reasoning Marius asked for): probably not, and that's
  fine. It's a read. With MTE on, the moment the read crosses into the neighboring allocation
  (which has a different color), the CPU crashes the program about 15 times out of 16. So
  the leak most likely turns into "the app just dies." To still pull it off, the attacker would need
  to learn the color first — and this is a remote video parser, the hardest place to do that.
  "MTE probably wins here" is itself a clean, publishable result.

  Drawback (state it openly): because it's only a read, "success" is weak (a leak, not
  control), and it measures MTE at its strongest. Good for proving the harness; less
  dramatic as a finding.


  Target B — Skia (CVE-2025-32318): the WRITE target
  What it is: a heap out-of-bounds write in Skia, Android's 2D graphics library. Crafted
  graphics input writes past a buffer and corrupts adjacent memory, leading to privilege
  escalation. Remote, no user interaction, Android 16, CVSS 8.8 (impact rated "total"). No
  public PoC.

  Why it's worth adding:

        It's a write, so "success" is a real security effect (taking control), not just a leak. This is
        the path MTE is actually designed to stop, so "can the agent get around it" is a meatier
        question.
        Skia processes untrusted graphics everywhere, so it's a genuinely important surface.
        Also C++ on ARM, on Scudo.

  Drawbacks (state them openly):



                                                                                                   Page 2 of 3

Target (T1)




        It's privilege-escalation-flavored, which sits nearer MTE's weaker end (where leaking
        the color is easier), so a win here is less impressive than beating MTE at its strong end.
        Skia is a big codebase — much harder to build and isolate than one small decoder. No
        public PoC or vulnerable-code detail yet.
        Open question for Marius: is the bug reached by remote rendered content, or only
        after the attacker already has a foothold? That answer decides whether Skia tests MTE
        at its strong or weak end.


  Why two targets, and in what order
  One read + one write covers both halves of what MTE does (catching bad reads and bad
  writes), and lets us say something general instead of a single data point. Admitting each
  one's drawback is part of what makes the write-up trustworthy.

  Order: dav1d first. It's the fastest to stand up, so it de-risks the harness and success-
  checker. Only once that machinery is proven do we add Skia for the write case. Not in
  parallel — that's how a two-target project stalls into two half-finished ones.

  1. Latest Project Zero findings — what do they say about
  vulnerabilities?
  Project Zero's "MTE As Implemented" series (Mark Brand) is the key read. Their bottom
  line: MTE is not a reliable hard wall — it's a speed bump whose height depends on
  context. They sort every bypass into two buckets:

         Known-tag: learn the tag (usually via a speculative/timing side channel), then your bad
         access carries the right tag and never faults. Wherever an attacker can build such a
         side channel, MTE's probabilistic protection fundamentally fails.
         Unknown-tag: succeed even with the wrong tag, by exploiting an implementation gap
         (async window, untagged memory, etc.).

  They also rank where MTE actually bites: weak against a local attacker who can run code
  (Chrome renderer), strong against a remote attacker hitting a media/file parser (a
  messaging app) — because that attacker can't easily build the side channel. The Pixel 10
  post adds a real example: a recent exploit chain only needed small tweaks to survive new
  hardware mitigations (PAC cost them one extra step, not a wall).




                                                                                           Page 2 of 5

Tasks




  2. Open vulnerabilities that could hypothetically be exploited
  (MTE/PA)
  Ways to skip the 1-in-15 guess:

        Side channels that leak the tag without crashing (TikTag, StickyTags for MTE; PACMAN
        for PA). The big one.
        Untagged memory — globals/ .data have no tag to mismatch; Android's zygote
        sharing makes pointer-forging across apps easy.
        Intra-granule overflow — a small overflow staying inside one 16-byte chunk shares the
        tag, so it's invisible.
        Check suppression — code inside Scudo's ScopedDisableMemoryTagChecks
        (PSTATE.TCO) runs with checks off; the question is whether attacker data reaches it.
        Async-mode window — the bad access is observable before the delayed fault lands.
        Tag exclusions — tag 0 excluded in Scudo (userspace); tag 15 bypasses checks in the
        kernel.
        Repeated attempts against an app that respawns without re-randomizing tags.

  PA-specific: short signatures (brute-forceable with an oracle), substitution (swap one
  validly-signed pointer for another), signing/auth oracles, and data-only attacks PA never
  covers.


  3. How Scudo works, and how it uses MTE
  Scudo is Android's default malloc / free implementation (since Android 11). A hardened
  allocator: fast size-class pools (primary), guard-paged large allocations (secondary), an 8-
  byte header with a 16-bit CRC checksum (not cryptographic, not a PAC), randomized
  placement, optional quarantine (off by default).

  How it uses MTE: MTE is the hardware mechanism — the CPU stores a 4-bit tag per 16-
  byte granule and checks it on every load/store, but it has no opinion on which tags to use.
  Scudo is the one that implements the policy on top of that mechanism: on each
  allocation it picks a random non-zero tag ( IRG ), stamps it across the allocation while
  zeroing it ( STZG / DC GZVA ), and returns the tagged pointer; on free it retags so stale
  pointers mismatch. Lock vs locksmith: MTE is the lock, Scudo assigns and changes the
  keys. (Confirmed from source: Scudo's tagging is MTE-only — no PA in it.)




                                                                                          Page 3 of 5

Tasks




  4. Our real-world target
  Lead: dav1d, CVE-2025-48592. A heap buffer overflow → out-of-bounds read in
  C2SoftDav1dDec.cpp , Android's AV1 video-decoder wrapper. Why it fits: it's C/C++ on
  ARM, runs on Scudo, is remote and zero-click (a crafted video triggers it, no user tap),
  affects Android 15/16, and has a patch commit to diff. It sits in the remote-parser context
  where Project Zero says MTE is strongest, which makes "can an agent beat it anyway" a
  genuinely open question.

  Exploitability under the hardened allocator: it's a read (info leak). With MTE SYNC on,
  the overread crosses into a differently-tagged neighbor and crashes ~15/16 of the time —
  so it most likely degrades from a leak to a crash, unless the overread stays within one 16-
  byte granule, or the attacker can learn the tag (hard, remotely). That "MTE probably wins
  here" is itself a publishable result.

  Backups: libaom (CVE-2024-5171, integer→heap overflow, another clean standalone C
  library) and Android Bluetooth SDP use-after-frees (CVE-2025-0084/0075/0074) — UAFs
  test temporal detection and give a clearer write-style "security effect" than an OOB read.
  Not better than dav1d overall, but worth having a UAF in the mix.


  5. The plan, step by step (simplified)
  The one question we're answering: how good is an LLM agent at finding and exploiting
  memory-safety bugs — and does a hardened allocator (Scudo + MTE) stop it? We start
  tiny and build up, so every result is honest.

   1. Prove the ruler works. Write a few deliberately-buggy C programs; confirm MTE
        catches what it should and lets valid runs through. Build the success-checker and
        logging before any agent.
   2. Measure the baselines. Run a dumb random-guesser and a normal fuzzer on those
        programs. Now we have numbers to beat.
   3. Bring in the agent. Same programs, same rules; vary what it's given (source, binary,
        crash logs). Compare to the baselines. Classify why it wins when it wins.
   4. Reproduce a known attack. Can the agent redo a published MTE bypass? (Kept
      separate from new tasks, since it may be in training data.)
   5. The real target. Point it at dav1d/CVE-2025-48592 under Scudo + MTE and reason +
      measure: does the bug survive the hardened allocator, and can the agent make it?




                                                                                            Page 4 of 5

Tasks




  Throughout: an independent checker decides success, we replay wins from clean state,
  and we report costs and failures too — not just the best run.


  6. Two targets: a read and a write (decision to confirm with Marius)
  We should use two real-world targets, one of each bug shape, because they stress
  different halves of what MTE does. State both drawbacks openly — that honesty is part of
  the contribution.

        Read target — dav1d (CVE-2025-48592). An out-of-bounds read (info leak). Tests
        whether MTE catches a bad read (spatial detection). Drawback: "success" is weak — a
        leak, and MTE most likely just turns it into a crash. It mostly measures MTE at its
        strongest (remote parser).
        Write target — Skia (CVE-2025-32318). An out-of-bounds write → privilege escalation.
        Tests the corruption-to-real-effect path MTE is actually built to stop, so "success" is a
        clear security win. Drawbacks: it's privilege-escalation-flavored, which sits nearer
        MTE's weaker end, and Skia is a big codebase that's much harder to build and isolate
        than one small decoder.

  Sequencing (important): do dav1d first — it's one self-contained decoder, so it's the
  fastest way to get the harness and success-checker working end to end. Only after that
  machinery is proven, add Skia for the write case. Don't start both in parallel; that's how the
  project stalls.

  Ask Marius: one target done deeply for a first result, or commit to both now? Bring it as a
  choice, not a done deal — it's a scope call that's his to make. Also ask: how is the Skia bug
  reached — remote-rendered content, or only after a local foothold? That answer decides
  whether Skia tests MTE at its strong or weak end.

MTE / Scudo Research — Pre-Meeting Handout
Prepared for internal discussion. Covers mitigation mechanics, the defensive research thesis,
verified platform facts, and the authorization path. Scope note: this document reasons about
how the mitigation works and how the research should be authorized and disclosed — it does
not contain exploit construction.

Topic 1 — How MTE tags work (the core concept)
Q: What is a pointer tag? Every MTE-protected pointer carries a 4-bit tag in its top byte. The
memory it points to is "painted" with a matching tag. On each dereference, the hardware
checks that the pointer's tag matches the memory's tag. Mismatch → fault.
Q: What is a "known" vs "unknown" tag, and why does it matter? From an attacker's point of
view, a tag is known if its value has been learned and unknown if it would have to be guessed.
Guessing is roughly 1-in-15 (tag 0 is excluded). This distinction is the entire hinge of MTE's
protection: acting on a pointer whose tag you don't know is a coin-flip that usually faults.
MTE's security guarantee rests on tags staying unknown. That single sentence is the thesis
of this research (see Topic 3).

Topic 2 — How Scudo implements tagging
Q: Does Scudo tag whole objects? Yes. One tag covers the entire allocation — a single tag
value is written across the whole chunk, so every 16-byte granule shares one color.
Consequence: MTE cannot see an overflow that stays inside one allocation (one field into
another of the same object); it only catches an access that crosses out into a differently-tagged
neighbor. (Source-confirmed.)
Q: Does Scudo pad allocations? Yes, necessarily. Tags apply at 16-byte granularity, so every
allocation is rounded up to a multiple of 16, and the slack shares the allocation's tag. Example:
ask for 20 bytes → 32-byte tagged region, with 12 bytes of same-tagged padding. Consequence:
an overflow landing within that padding is invisible to MTE — it has to reach past the padding
into the next allocation to fault. (16-byte alignment source-confirmed; padding consequence is
the direct logical follow-on, also in Android docs.)
Q: When does Scudo retag? On free / reallocation. When a chunk is freed and later handed
back out, Scudo assigns it a new tag. The old dangling pointer keeps the old tag; the memory
now has a new one; mismatch → fault. This is the use-after-free catch. Nuance: retagging
happens on reuse, and the quarantine that would delay reuse is off by default in Scudo — so
there's no cooling-off period and reuse can happen quickly. (Source-confirmed in concept.)
Q: What is the next-tag-picking strategy? Two layers:

Hardware: the tag-generating instruction picks a random tag subject to an exclude mask.
     Scudo always excludes tag 0, giving a uniform draw from the 15 non-zero values. (Source-
     confirmed.)
     Policy (Android M_MEMTAG_TUNING ): the default, BUFFER_OVERFLOW , forces a new
     allocation's tag to differ from its neighbors', so a linear overflow is caught
     deterministically (always, not 14/15) — at some cost to UAF coverage. The alternative,
      UAF , uses fully random tags for even ~1-in-15 coverage of both cases. (Doc-sourced —
     confirm against the pinned Scudo commit; tag-picking policy is exactly the kind of thing
     docs get subtly wrong.)
Q: Is MTE on by default in Scudo? No. Scudo has been the system allocator since Android 11
and supports MTE, but it only tags allocations if MTE is enabled for the process. On a stock
Pixel 8 it is off by default (opt-in). The machinery is dormant until something turns it on.
Q: How do you opt in? Layered, app down to syscall:
     App manifest: android:memtagMode="sync" (or async ).
     Build / platform: PRODUCT_MEMTAG_HEAP_SYNC_INCLUDE_PATHS ; sanitize: {
     memtag_heap: true } in Android.bp .
     System properties (for experimentation): arm64.memtag.process.<name>=sync , or
     device-wide persist.arm64.memtag.app_default=sync .
     Under the hood: all of these bottom out in prctl(PR_SET_TAGGED_ADDR_CTRL, …) with
     the SYNC flag. (Bottom layer source-confirmed; higher layers doc-sourced.)
Audit to-do: verify the doc-sourced items (especially the tuning policy) against your pinned
Scudo commit, and pin the commit since main drifts from any shipped build.

Topic 3 — The research thesis (defensive framing)
Q: What is the central research question? MTE converts memory-safety bugs into
probabilistic faults. Its guarantee holds only because tags stay unknown to the attacker. So
the question that actually matters is: what capability would make tags knowable — and what
detection or hardening removes that capability?
Q: Why frame it this way? Because the valuable, publishable, authorizable finding is the
threat model, not a working bypass. You can state precisely what a deterministic tag-leak
primitive would mean for MTE's guarantees, and what would blunt it (e.g., quarantine-on,
tuning choices, leak-surface reduction, detection of repeated probing), without building the
leak. This is the version of the work that survives outside review.
Q: What are the defensive follow-ups to raise in the meeting?

Which Scudo/Android configuration choices most weaken the "tags stay unknown"
      assumption (quarantine default, tuning mode)?
      What would detection of tag-probing behavior look like at the allocator or OS level?
      How much does each hardening option cost in performance vs. coverage?

Topic 4 — Platform facts (verified)
Question                          Answer

Do the relevant component         Yes — both have bugs present on Android 16. (Confirm exact CVE IDs
bugs (dav1d, Skia) exist on the   and affected-version ranges against the AOSP Security Bulletin before

Does the platform use Scudo?      Yes — Scudo is the system allocator (since Android 11).

                                  paths above.


One-line to say in the meeting: "Version references are consistent — Scudo has been the
allocator since Android 11; Android 16 is our target OS; Pixel 8 is the MTE-capable hardware."

Topic 5 — Authorization path (do this first)
Q: Why does authorization order matter? Mitigation-bypass research is legitimate and
valuable — but the credible version secures authorization and a disclosure path before doing
the work, not after. Capability-first-then-authorization is the pattern to avoid.
Q: What are the three authorization mechanisms?
      Institutional sign-off — written approval from whoever owns the risk (manager, PI,
      security lead, legal/compliance), defining scope and an accountable owner. For academic
      work this routes through ethics/security review.
      VRP scope (Vulnerability Rewards Program) — the vendor's published invitation to do
      this class of research under rules they define, with coordinated disclosure and (inside
      scope) safe-harbor protection. This is the natural home for MTE/Scudo mitigation
      research.

Research agreement — a formal contract for work beyond public VRP terms (pre-release
     builds, deeper access, longer embargo).
Q: What's the concrete fit here — the Android VRP?
     Google runs the Android and Google Devices Security Reward Program (ASR),
     covering AOSP, Pixel devices, and Chrome.
     It explicitly rewards full exploit chains on current Pixel hardware, with top rewards
     substantially increased in the recent overhaul (up to seven figures for the highest-impact
     chains).
     Notably, the recent program update explicitly prizes vulnerability classes that AI tools
     struggle with, and names AI model-interaction safety as a focus area — which is
     directly relevant to the "can a model help here" question (and is the authorized,
     disclosure-oriented way to explore it).
     Chrome's own VRP has deprioritized standalone renderer RCE and arbitrary read/write,
     steering researchers toward full, high-impact chains reported through the program.
Pre-meeting action: read the current ASR rules page (bughunters.google.com) and bring a
one-paragraph summary of in-scope targets and the disclosure process, so you can propose
authorization-first as the way this proceeds.
Sources: Google Security Blog (ASR program announcements and VRP year-in-review); Help
Net Security and industry coverage of the 2024–2025 Google VRP overhaul; Google Bug
Hunters program rules.

Your pre-meeting checklist
  1. Scudo/MTE mechanics — done (Topics 1–2); finish the source-vs-docs audit and pin the
     commit.
  2. Threat-model writeup — done (Topic 3); be ready to present the "tags stay unknown"
     thesis and the defensive follow-ups.
  3. Platform facts — verified (Topic 4); confirm exact CVE IDs against the AOSP bulletin.
  4. Authorization path — read the ASR rules and bring the one-paragraph scope summary
     (Topic 5).
Not on the list: probing a model for exploit output or mapping its safety limits. That isn't a
presentable deliverable and the authorization-first path above is what replaces it.
